newsitem.title: TOGO: OAU foreign ministers seek Zaire solution.
newsitem.headline: OAU foreign ministers seek Zaire solution.

text.p: Organisation of African Unity (OAU) foreign ministers met in Togo on Tuesday to agree ways of brokering peace in Zaire's civil war, with international lobbying for a truce and negotiations intensifying.

Officials said proposals from the ministers would be put to heads of state in Lome on Wednesday at a special summit, dismissed by critics as a ploy by French-speaking Africa to rescue veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Laurent Kabila's rebels now control about a quarter of Africa's third-largest country.

A rebel delegation will attend their first major international forum but with neither Kabila himself nor Mobutu nor Uganda's regional power broker Yoweri Museveni present it was unclear what new ground, if any, the summit would break.
Pierre Koffi Panou, host foreign minister, opened the meeting saying it was a test of the credibility and efficiency of the OAU.
"The tragedy in Zaire is an illustration of a new form of conflict which, following the Cold War, threatens our whole continent," he told delegates.
France and the United States, who have both sent troops to the region to evacuate their nationals if the need arises, have joined forces to lobby for a truce and talks.

South African sources said on Monday Kabila had softened his previous demand to negotiate with Mobutu alone. Kabila has accepted talks with delegates formally mandated by Mobutu to reach a settlement, the sources said.
Mobutu's reply to the proposal, conveyed by South African emissaries last Sunday, is expected by Tuesday night, South African and Zairean sources said.

Kabila's aides said on Monday he would not attend the Lome summit for security reasons. They did not elaborate but Togo's President Gnassingbe Eyadema is one of Mobutu's closest allies. Neither Mobutu's nor Zaire's delegates had arrived by Tuesday morning.
The ailing Mobutu, in a statement before he returned to Zaire on Friday after fresh cancer treatment in Europe, called for a ceasefire before talks.
South Africa's vice-president, Thabo Mbeki, said after meeting Mobutu on Sunday that the focus of diplomatic efforts to end the war was a truce and talks.
Mobutu, 66, seized power in Zaire in 1965 and has dominated the sprawling former Belgian colony at the heart of Africa since then.
But Kabila's revolt, which erupted in October while Mobutu was in Europe recovering from prostate cancer surgery, has drastically changed the balance of power.

Mobutu's army has collapsed in the face of determined rebel thrusts on several fronts. On Monday night Zaire's prime minister, Kengo wa Dondo, resigned after opposition parties in the transitional parliament passed a motion condemning him for mishandling the war and dealings with the rebels.
Many ordinary Zaireans say they are eager for change after three decades of poverty under Mobutu's rule.
From the poor quarters of the teeming capital Kinshasa to autonomy-hungry Lubumbashi in the southern mining province of Shaba, they openly welcome the prospect of the rebels' arrival.
Mohamed Sahnoun, the joint OAU-United Nations special representative on the Great Lakes crisis, was in Lome for the summit.
